 USDA seeks to curb fraud through EBT card security requirements
 USDA’s proposed rule answers a longstanding call to upgrade EBT cards with chip technology, but now some are wondering, who will pay for it?
 Justin Doubleday @jdoubledayWFED 
 November 2, 2026 6:15 pm 
 4 min read 
 The Agriculture Department is taking steps to prevent fraudsters from stealing Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program benefits by advancing rules that would require state-issued benefits cards to include modern security features.
 Under a proposed rule released last month, USDA will require state SNAP agencies to upgrade their Electronic Benefit Transfer cards to use chip and near-field communication (NFC) technology. It would also require SNAP retailers to accept EBT transactions using chip and NFC technology.
 The use of such technology is standard in most modern credit and debit cards.
 “Based on the experience of the consumer payment industry, the department believes EBT cards utilizing chip and NFC technology will significantly reduce SNAP benefit theft due to the enhanced security features that mitigate skimming and cloning attacks,” the Food and Nutrition Service wrote in a summary of the proposed rule.

 For years, fraud and security experts have warned that the lack of chip technology in EBT cards leaves beneficiaries susceptible to card skimming, cloning and other digital fraud. The 2023 appropriations bill required USDA to issue regulations with new security standards to prevent SNAP benefit theft.
 In a January report, USDA’s Office of Inspector General found that the lack of security features in SNAP cards led to FNS replacing $322 million in benefits, “likely due to fraudulent activity,” between October 2022 and December 2024.
 The OIG also projected that without any updates to chip technology, SNAP benefits would be subject to an additional $233 million in fraudulent activity over fiscal 2025 and 2026.
 The use of card skimming and cloning has grown more rampant. Last month, eight people were accused of using stolen SNAP information to create EBT card clones, which allowed them to allegedly steal more than $7 million in benefits from low-income New Yorkers.
 The proposed rule , which is out for comment until Dec. 22, would also establish SNAP EBT operating standards.
 The standards could be revised on an ongoing basis, USDA explains, allowing the department “to revise EBT requirements more dynamically in response to rapidly evolving payment technology and best practices in the consumer payment industry.”
 In the rule itself, USDA proposes that state agencies ensure their EBT systems align with specifications maintained by the Accredited Standards Committee within 180 days of any updates. FNS began working with that committee in 2023 to align SNAP EBT technology with standards in the credit and debit industry.

 In a September 2026 white paper, ATARC’s Fraud Detection and Mitigation Working Group made the case for chip-enabled EBT cards along with stronger point-of-sale controls. It also said policymakers should focus on application fraud, such as identity misrepresentation and cross-state duplicate enrollment, as well.
 Eight states have already starting issuing chip-enabled EBT cards. And New York and Pennsylvania have also announced plans to issue new chip-enabled cards next year. They are among seven other states that USDA lists as “in progress” toward EBT chip cards.
 The states that have adopted chip technology and other improvements have reported major progress in stamping out EBT fraud. California, for instance, said it reduced EBT theft by 83% by introducing chip and tap technology along with PIN resets, targeted law enforcement investigations, predictive theft modeling and new online services for users.
 Implementation questions
 While the push to upgrade card technology is widely supported, there are plenty of implementation questions. USDA, in its summary of the proposed rule acknowledges that “households will be required to activate these new chip cards upon receipt, and households experiencing homelessness may need to travel to a local office to obtain their new card.”
 And the Aspen Institute, in a report issued after USDA’s proposed rule was released, cautioned that the dozens of states that have yet to adopt chip technology won’t be able to fund the security upgrades alone.
 “Modernizing EBT payment systems is a complex and costly undertaking, requiring states to upgrade technology, negotiate changes with EBT processors, coordinate with retailers, and help cardholders navigate new security features without disrupting access to benefits,” the authors of the report write.
 The One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBA) increased states’ share of SNAP administrative costs to 75%, up from the previous 50%, while also expanding work requirements for SNAP and Medicaid beneficiaries.
 Aspen points to a survey of 39 states released by the American Public Human Services Association that found 58% of them reported shifting resources away from other priorities to improve payment accuracy requirements in the OBBBA, including 13% that had delayed investments in EBT chip cards.
 The Aspen report urges Congress to consider funding to support states’ implementation of the security upgrades.
          Read more: IT Modernization 
 In its proposed rule, USDA estimated that the new requirements would result in a one-time cost totaling $283 million in fiscal 2028 and 2029 for state agencies, the federal government, households and businesses that have to support transactions with the new cards.
 USDA’s rule doesn’t break out how much of the costs would be borne by the states versus the federal government.
 “USDA’s proposal represents meaningful progress,” the Aspen Institute authors write. “Establishing modern security standards across SNAP can help close a gap that has left millions of households vulnerable to theft. But a regulation alone cannot pay for new cards, upgrade payment infrastructure, or give states the capacity to implement and maintain stronger security systems.”
